      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HBV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions.</p>What is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> is a type of <span class="qt3">viral</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span>. It can cause an acute (short-term) or <span class="qt0">chronic</span> (long-term) <span class="qt4">infection</span>. People with an acute <span class="qt4">infection</span> usually get better on their own without treatment. Some people with <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> will need treatment.</p><p>Thanks to a vaccine, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> is not very common in the United States. It is more common in certain parts of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.</p>What causes <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> is caused by the <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> <span class="qt3">virus. The virus</span> spreads through contact with blood, semen, or other body fluids from a person who has the <span class="qt3">virus</span>.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, but the risk is higher in:</p><ul><li>Infants born to mothers who have <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span></li><li>People who inject drugs or share needles, syringes, and other types of drug equipment</li><li>Sex partners of people with <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, especially if they are not using latex or polyurethane condoms during sex</li><li>Men who have sex with men</li><li>People who live with someone who has <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, especially if they use the same razor, toothbrush, or nail clippers</li><li>Health care and public-safety workers who are exposed to blood on the job</li><li>Hemodialysis patients</li><li>People who have lived in or traveled often to parts of the world where <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> is common</li><li>People who have diabetes, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, or <span class="qt3">HIV</span></li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>?<p>Often, people with <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> don't have symptoms. Adults and children over 5 are more likely to have symptoms than younger children.</p><p>Some people with acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> have symptoms 2 to 5 months after <span class="qt4">infection</span>. These symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Yellowish eyes and skin, called jaundice</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, you may not have symptoms until complications develop. This could be decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> screening is important, even if you have no symptoms. Screening means that you are tested for a disease even though you don't have symptoms. If you are at high risk, your health care provider may suggest  screening.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> cause?<p>In rare cases, acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> can cause liver failure.</p><p><span class="qt0">Chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> can develop into a serious disease that causes long-term health problems such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and liver failure.</p><p>If you have ever had <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, the <span class="qt3">virus</span> may become active again, or reactivated, later in life. This could start to damage the liver and cause symptoms.</p>How is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A physical exam</li><li>Blood tests, including tests for <span class="qt3">viral</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span></li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>?<p>If you have acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span>, you probably don't need treatment. Some people with <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> don't need treatment. But if you have a <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span> and blood tests show that <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> could be damaging your liver, you may need to take <span class="qt3">antiviral</span> medicines.</p>Can <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> is to get the <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> vaccine.</p><p>You can also reduce your chance of <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span> by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools</li><li>Not sharing personal items, such as toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>If you think you have been in contact with the <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> <span class="qt3">virus</span>, see your health care provider right away. Your provider may give you a dose of the <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> vaccine to prevent <span class="qt4">infection</span>. In some cases, your provider may also give you a medicine called <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> <span class="qt2">B</span> immune globulin (HBIG). You need to get the vaccine and the HBIG (if needed) as soon as possible after coming into contact with the <span class="qt3">virus</span>. It is best if you can get them within 24 hours.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> C</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HCV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C?<p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. Inflammation can damage organs.</p><p>There are different types of <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span>. One type, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, is caused by the <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C <span class="qt3">virus</span> (HCV). <span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> C can range from a mild illness lasting a few weeks to a serious, lifelong illness.</p><p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> C can be acute or <span class="qt0">chronic</span>:</p><ul><li>Acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C is a short-term <span class="qt4">infection</span>. The symptoms can last up to 6 months. Sometimes your body is able to fight off the <span class="qt4">infection</span> and the <span class="qt3">virus</span> goes away. But for most people, an acute <span class="qt4">infection</span> leads to <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>.</li><li><span class="qt0">Chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C is a long-lasting <span class="qt4">infection</span>. If it is not treated, it can last for a lifetime and cause serious health problems, including liver damage, cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and even death.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C spread?<p><span class="qt1">Hepatitis</span> C spreads through contact with the blood of someone who has HCV. This contact may be through:</p><ul><li>Sharing drug needles or other drug materials with someone who has HCV. In the United States, this is the most common way that people get <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C.</li><li>Getting an accidental stick with a needle that was used on someone who has HCV. This can happen in health care settings.</li><li>Being tattooed or pierced with tools or inks that were not sterilized after being used on someone who has HCV.</li><li>Having contact with the blood or open sores of someone who has HCV.</li><li>Sharing personal care items that may have come in contact with another person's blood, such as razors or toothbrushes.</li><li>Being born to a mother with HCV.</li><li>Having unprotected sex with someone who has HCV.</li></ul><p>Before 1992, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C was also commonly spread through blood transfusions and organ transplants. Since then, there has been routine testing of the U.S. blood supply for HCV. It is now very rare for someone to get HCV this way.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C?<p>You are more likely to get <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C if you:</p><ul><li>Have injected drugs</li><li>Had a blood transfusion or organ transplant before July 1992</li><li>Have hemophilia and received clotting factor before 1987</li><li>Have been on kidney dialysis</li><li>Have been in contact with blood or infected needles at work</li><li>Have had tattoos or body piercings</li><li>Have worked or lived in a prison</li><li>Were born to a mother with <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C</li><li>Have <span class="qt3">HIV</span></li><li>Have had more than one sex partner in the last 6 months</li><li>Have had a sexually transmitted <span class="qt4">infection</span> (STI)</li><li>Are a man who has had sex with men (MSM)</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, your health care provider will likely recommend that you get tested for it.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Most people with <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C have no symptoms. Some people with acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C do have symptoms within 1 to 3 months after they are exposed to the <span class="qt3">virus</span>. These symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Pain in your abdomen (belly)</li><li>Jaundice (yellowish eyes and skin)</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, you probably will not have symptoms until it causes complications. This can happen decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C screening is important, even if you have no symptoms.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C cause?<p>Without treatment, <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C may lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. Early diagnosis and treatment of <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C can prevent these complications.</p>How is <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C diagnosed?<p>Providers diagnose <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C based on your medical history, a physical exam, and blood tests.</p><p>If you do have <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, you may need additional tests to check for liver damage. These tests may include other blood tests, an ultrasound of the liver, and a liver biopsy.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C is with <span class="qt3">antiviral</span> medicines. They can cure the disease in most cases.</p><p>If you have acute <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C, your provider may wait to see if your <span class="qt4">infection</span> becomes <span class="qt0">chronic</span> before starting treatment.</p><p>If your <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C causes cirrhosis, you should see a doctor who specializes in liver diseases. Treatments for health problems related to cirrhosis include medicines, surgery, and other medical procedures. If your <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C leads to liver failure or liver cancer, you may need a liver transplant.</p>Can <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine for <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C. But you can help protect yourself from <span class="qt1">hepatitis</span> C <span class="qt4">infection</span> by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials.</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores.</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools and unopened ink.</li><li>Not sharing personal items such toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers.</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt3">HIV</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">AIDS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Human Immunodeficiency <span class="qt3">Virus</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt3">HIV</span>?<p><span class="qt3">HIV</span> stands for human immunodeficiency <span class="qt3">virus. HIV</span> harms your immune system by destroying a type of white blood cell that helps your body fight <span class="qt4">infection</span>. This puts you at risk for other <span class="qt4">infections</span> and diseases.</p>What is AIDS?<p>AIDS stands for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. It is the final stage of <span class="qt4">infection</span> with <span class="qt3">HIV</span>. It happens when the body's immune system is badly damaged because of the <span class="qt3">virus</span>. Not everyone with <span class="qt3">HIV</span> develops AIDS.</p>How does <span class="qt3">HIV</span> spread?<p><span class="qt3">HIV</span> is spread through certain body fluids from a person who has <span class="qt3">HIV</span>. This can happen:</p><ul><li>By having unprotected vaginal or anal sex with a person who has <span class="qt3">HIV</span>. "Unprotected" means not using condoms or medicine to treat or prevent <span class="qt3">HIV</span>. This is the most common way that it spreads.</li><li>By sharing drug needles.</li><li>Through contact with the blood of a person with <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</li><li>From mother to fetus during pregnancy.</li><li>From mother to baby during, childbirth, or breastfeeding.</li></ul>Who is at risk for <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt3">HIV</span>, but certain groups have a higher risk of getting it:</p><ul><li>People who have another sexually transmitted <span class="qt4">infection</span> (STI). Having an STI can increase your risk of getting or spreading <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</li><li>People who inject drugs with shared needles.</li><li>Gay and bisexual men.</li><li>Black/African Americans and Hispanic/Latino Americans. They make up a higher proportion of new <span class="qt3">HIV</span> diagnoses and people with <span class="qt3">HIV</span>, compared to other races and ethnicities.</li><li>People who engage in risky sexual behaviors, such as not using condoms or medicine to prevent or treat <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</li></ul><p>Factors such as stigma, discrimination, income, education, and geographic region can also affect people's risk for <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt3">HIV</span>?<p>The first signs of <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span> may be flu-like symptoms:</p><ul><li>Fever</li><li>Chills</li><li>Rash</li><li>Night sweats (heavy sweating during sleep)</li><li>Muscle aches</li><li>Sore throat</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Swollen lymph nodes</li><li>Mouth ulcers</li></ul><p>These symptoms may come and go within two to four weeks. This stage is called acute <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>.</p><p>If the <span class="qt4">infection</span> is not treated, it becomes <span class="qt0">chronic</span> <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>. Often, there are no symptoms during this stage. If it is not treated, eventually the <span class="qt3">virus</span> will weaken your body's immune system. Then the <span class="qt4">infection</span> will progress to AIDS. This is the late stage of <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>. Because your immune system is badly damaged, your body cannot fight off other <span class="qt4">infections</span>, called opportunistic <span class="qt4">infections</span> (OIs). OIs are <span class="qt4">infections</span> that happen more frequently or are more severe in people who have weakened immune systems.</p><p>Some people may not feel sick during the earlier stages of <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>. So the only way to know for sure whether you have <span class="qt3">HIV</span> is to get tested.</p>How do I know if I have <span class="qt3">HIV</span>?<p>A blood test can tell if you have <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>. Your health care provider can do the test, or you can use a home testing kit. You can also use the CDC Testing Locator to find free testing sites.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt3">HIV</span>?<p>There is no cure for <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span>, but it can be treated with medicines. This is called antiretroviral therapy (ART).  ART can make <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span> a manageable <span class="qt0">chronic</span> condition. It also reduces the risk of spreading the <span class="qt3">virus</span> to others.</p><p>Most people with <span class="qt3">HIV</span> live long and healthy lives if they get ART as soon as possible and stay on it. It's also important to take care of yourself. Making sure that you have the support you need, living a healthy lifestyle, and getting regular medical care can help you enjoy a better quality of life.</p>Can <span class="qt3">HIV</span> <span class="qt4">infection</span> be prevented?<p>You can reduce the risk of getting or spreading <span class="qt3">HIV</span> by:</p><ul><li>Getting tested for <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</li><li>Choosing less risky sexual behaviors. This includes limiting the number of sexual partners you have and using latex condoms every time you have sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li><li>Getting tested and treated for sexually transmitted <span class="qt4">infections</span> (STIs).</li><li>Not injecting drugs.</li><li>Talking to your provider about medicines to prevent <span class="qt3">HIV</span>:
	<ul><li>PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who don't already have <span class="qt3">HIV</span> but are at very high risk of getting it. PrEP is daily medicine that can reduce this risk.</li><li>PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) is for people who have possibly been exposed to <span class="qt3">HIV</span>. It is only for emergency situations. PEP must be started within 72 hours after a possible exposure to <span class="qt3">HIV</span>.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institutes of Health</p></content>
